questions.question: What is a direct object?
options: A noun or pronoun that receives the action of the verb
A word that tells to whom or for whom the action is done
A word that completes an intransitive verb
A verb that does not need an object
questions.explanation: A direct object is defined as a noun or pronoun that receives the action of the verb.

questions.question: Which question helps identify the direct object of a verb?
questions.explanation: A direct object is identified by asking who or what in relation to the verb.

questions.question: What does an indirect object tell us?
options: To whom or for whom the action is performed
questions.explanation: An indirect object is a noun or pronoun that tells us to whom or for whom the action of the verb is performed.

questions.question: Which question is used to identify an indirect object?
questions.explanation: An indirect object answers the question to whom or for whom the action is done.

questions.question: True or False: An indirect object can exist in a sentence without a direct object.
questions.explanation: The text states that for a verb to have an indirect object, there must also be a direct object.

questions.question: In a sentence with both objects, where does the indirect object usually appear?
options: At the end of the sentence
questions.explanation: The indirect object usually appears before the direct object.

questions.question: How can you reverse the usual order of direct and indirect objects?
options: By using a preposition such as to or for with the indirect object
By changing the verb to passive
By placing the indirect object after the verb
questions.explanation: The order can be reversed by using a preposition (to, for) with the indirect object.

questions.question: In 'She gave me a book,' what is 'me'?
questions.explanation: 'Me' tells to whom the book was given, so it is the indirect object.

questions.question: In 'He brought her some flowers,' what is 'some flowers'?
questions.explanation: 'Some flowers' receives the action of the verb brought, so it is the direct object.

questions.question: In 'My father gifted me a nice watch,' what is 'me'?
questions.explanation: 'Me' tells to whom the watch was gifted, so it is the indirect object.

questions.question: In 'Shala stitched a dress for her baby sister,' what is 'a dress'?
questions.explanation: 'A dress' receives the action of stitching, so it is the direct object.

questions.question: In 'Deepak lent his friend his binoculars,' what is 'his binoculars'?
questions.explanation: 'His binoculars' is the thing being lent, so it is the direct object.

questions.question: In 'Renu fed her dog biscuits,' what is 'her dog'?
questions.explanation: 'Her dog' tells to whom the biscuits were fed, so it is the indirect object.

questions.question: In 'He bought me an expensive pen,' what is 'an expensive pen'?
questions.explanation: 'An expensive pen' is the thing bought, so it is the direct object.

questions.question: In 'The judge awarded the criminal a life sentence,' what is 'the criminal'?
questions.explanation: 'The criminal' tells to whom the sentence was awarded, so it is the indirect object.

questions.question: In 'They sent you a mail,' what is 'a mail'?
questions.explanation: 'A mail' is the thing sent, so it is the direct object.

questions.question: In 'My mother taught me English,' what is 'me'?
questions.explanation: 'Me' tells to whom English was taught, so it is the indirect object.

questions.question: In 'She showed us all the gifts,' what is 'us'?
questions.explanation: 'Us' tells to whom the gifts were shown, so it is the indirect object.

questions.question: In 'Ranjini sold her old typewriter to the antique collector,' what is the direct object?
questions.explanation: 'Her old typewriter' is the thing sold, so it is the direct object.

questions.question: In 'Prem saw a rare species of vulture on his travels,' what is the direct object?
questions.explanation: 'A rare species of vulture' receives the action of saw, so it is the direct object.

questions.question: In 'We walked on the beach and ate ice creams,' which verb is transitive?
questions.explanation: 'Ate' is transitive because 'ice creams' is its direct object; 'walked' is intransitive.

questions.question: What is a transitive verb?
options: A verb that needs an object to complete its meaning
A verb that never takes an object
A verb that only appears in passive voice
A word that describes a noun
questions.explanation: A transitive verb is a verb which needs an object to complete its meaning.

questions.question: What is an intransitive verb?
options: A verb that makes complete sense by itself without an object
A verb that always takes two objects
A verb that needs an object
A verb that links a subject to a complement
questions.explanation: An intransitive verb makes complete sense by itself and does not need an object.

questions.question: In 'They bought some vegetables,' why is 'bought' transitive?
options: Because vegetables is the direct object
Because it is in past tense
questions.explanation: 'Bought' has the direct object 'vegetables', so it is transitive.

questions.question: In 'The race began,' why is 'began' intransitive?
options: Because it does not need an object to make complete sense
Because it has an indirect object
Because began is a linking verb
questions.explanation: The sentence makes complete sense without an object, so 'began' is intransitive.

questions.question: Which sentence has an intransitive verb?
options: The cat is sleeping on the couch.
questions.explanation: 'Sleeping' does not take an object, so it is intransitive.

questions.question: Which sentence has a transitive verb?
options: The rabbit is going into its burrow.
questions.explanation: 'Boils' has the object 'eggs', so it is transitive in this sentence.

questions.question: What does the 'Watch Out!' section teach about some verbs?
options: The same verb can be transitive or intransitive depending on how it is used.
All verbs are either always transitive or always intransitive.
Intransitive verbs cannot be used in the past tense.
Transitive verbs do not need objects.
questions.explanation: The same verbs can be transitive or intransitive, depending on how the verb is used.

questions.question: In 'Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius,' the verb 'boils' is:
questions.explanation: There is no object, so 'boils' is intransitive here.

questions.question: In 'Mother boils eggs for breakfast,' the verb 'boils' is:
questions.explanation: 'Eggs' is the direct object, so 'boils' is transitive here.

questions.question: What is a verb of incomplete predication?
options: An intransitive verb that needs other words to complete its meaning
A verb that always has a direct object
A verb that cannot be used in questions
A verb that shows strong emotion
questions.explanation: Intransitive verbs which need words other than objects to complete their meaning are called intransitive verbs of incomplete predication.

questions.question: In 'Sanjay seems angry,' why is 'seems' a verb of incomplete predication?
options: Because it needs 'angry' to complete the meaning
Because it has a direct object
Because it is in past tense
questions.explanation: 'Seems' needs the complement 'angry' to complete the meaning of the sentence.

questions.question: What is a subjective complement?
options: A word that completes the meaning of a verb and tells about the subject
A word that receives the action of the verb
A word that tells to whom the action is done
A verb that does not need an object
questions.explanation: Subjective complements give information about the subject of a sentence.

questions.question: In 'King Krishnadeva Raya was wise,' what is 'wise'?
questions.explanation: 'Wise' tells us about the subject and completes the meaning of 'was', so it is a subjective complement.

questions.question: What is an objective complement?
options: A word that gives information about the object of the verb
A word that gives information about the subject
A word that receives the action
A verb that needs no object
questions.explanation: Complements that give information about the object of the verb are called objective complements.

questions.question: In 'The prince appointed him minister,' what is 'minister'?
questions.explanation: 'Minister' tells us what the man was appointed as, so it is an objective complement.

questions.question: In 'Pritha found the extra classes useful,' what is 'useful'?
questions.explanation: 'Useful' tells us how Pritha found the classes, so it is an objective complement.

questions.question: Which statement is true according to the chapter?
options: Transitive verbs too can take complements.
Only intransitive verbs can take complements.
questions.explanation: The text states that transitive verbs too take complements.

questions.question: A complement of a verb can be which of the following?
options: A noun, an adjective, or an adverb
questions.explanation: The text says the complement can be a noun, an adjective, or an adverb.

questions.question: In 'The little boy became a hero,' what is 'a hero'?
questions.explanation: 'A hero' tells us what the little boy became, so it is a subjective complement.

questions.question: In 'He saw three woodcutters,' the verb 'saw' is:
questions.explanation: 'Three woodcutters' is the direct object, so 'saw' is transitive.

questions.question: In 'The surgeon is very skillful,' what is 'skillful'?
questions.explanation: 'Skillful' tells us about the subject, so it is a subjective complement.

questions.question: In 'I found the conversation disturbing,' what is 'disturbing'?
questions.explanation: 'Disturbing' tells us about the object 'conversation', so it is an objective complement.

questions.question: In 'They are theatre artists,' what is 'theatre artists'?
questions.explanation: 'Theatre artists' tells us what the subject is, so it is a subjective complement.

questions.question: In 'He cannot reach the jar on the top shelf,' the verb 'reach' is:
questions.explanation: 'The jar' is the direct object, so 'reach' is transitive.

questions.question: In 'I will meet you at the guest house,' the verb 'meet' is:
questions.explanation: 'You' is the direct object, so 'meet' is transitive.

questions.question: In 'The detective found the ruined building empty,' what is 'empty'?
questions.explanation: 'Empty' tells us about the object 'building', so it is an objective complement.

questions.question: In 'I invited my cousins to my house,' the verb 'invited' is:
questions.explanation: 'My cousins' is the direct object, so 'invited' is transitive.

questions.question: In 'The little boy stood still,' the verb 'stood' is:
questions.explanation: 'Stood' does not take an object, so it is intransitive.

questions.question: In 'Officers immediately caught them,' the verb 'caught' is:
questions.explanation: 'Them' is the direct object, so 'caught' is transitive.
